title: Remove Duplicates, Keep First-Seen Order
statement:
`HashSet` removes duplicates but makes no promise at all about what order
it iterates its elements in -- that order comes from where each value
lands in the hash table, not from when it was inserted. `LinkedHashSet`
is the same deduping `Set` contract with one addition: it also threads a
linked list through its entries in insertion order, and iterates that
instead. For "deduplicate, keep first-seen order", that is not a
workaround -- it is exactly what the type is for.

## Your function

```
public static List<Integer> dedupePreserveOrder(List<Integer> values);
```

Return `values` with every element after its first occurrence removed, in
the same order the surviving elements first appeared in `values`.
`values` may be empty.

## Watch out

- **`new HashSet<>(values)` would deduplicate correctly and scramble the
  order.** It is the easy type to reach for out of habit, and the bug it
  introduces will not show up on a small, lucky test by hand -- only on
  data where the "wrong" order is visibly different from the right one.
- **`new LinkedHashSet<>(values)` does the entire job -- deduplicating
  *and* preserving first-seen order -- in one constructor call.** Feeding
  it `values` in order inserts each element once (a `Set`'s own contract
  silently rejects a second `add` of an equal value) and its iteration
  order is exactly that insertion order.
- **The return type is `List<Integer>`, not a `Set`.** `new
  ArrayList<>(theLinkedHashSet)` converts it back, walking the set in its
  (insertion) order to build the list -- this conversion is not where
  order could go wrong, since it is the last step, not the deduplication
  itself.

generator.source:
"""Random arrays over a small alphabet of values, so repeats are frequent
and the first-seen order is meaningfully tested."""


def generate(rng, count):
    return [_case(rng, i + 1) for i in range(count)]


def _case(rng, index):
    n = rng.randint(0, 20)
    values = [rng.randint(0, 6) for _ in range(n)]
    lines = [str(n)] + [str(v) for v in values]
    return {"name": "%d values from a small pool, repeats likely #%d"
                    % (n, index),
            "stdin": " ".join(lines) + "\n"}

tests.name: every element is the same value
order follows first appearance, not numeric order
tests.description: 3 appears first even though 1 and 2 are smaller -- the result is not sorted, and a plain HashSet would not reliably preserve this order either.
